subject: english
prompt: Grandpa is in the children's park with his paper-cone of peanuts. Tap the place where **Ravi** hid so that Grandpa would not see him.

image.alt: A children's park scene with a swing, a bench, an elephant-shaped bush and some people, with numbered markers

hint: Ravi had to bend low behind something green and leafy.
explanation: In the park Ravi had to **crouch** (bend the body low) behind a bush trimmed in the shape of an **elephant**. A small child thought he was playing hide and seek, and when Ravi said 'Shhh', the child's mother scolded him and waved her umbrella. Ravi finally had to crawl out of the park on all fours.

subject: english
prompt: The story opens with Ravi's mother putting tablets on a saucer and wishing that someone would invent **'Vitamin-M'**. What did she want it to do?

image.alt: Coloured tablets on a saucer beside a medicine bottle

options.text: Improve old people's memories, since Grandpa had become forgetful
Sharpen Grandpa's weak eyesight and hearing
Help Ravi concentrate on his studies during the holidays
Replace all the coloured tablets Grandpa had to take

hint: What could the letter M stand for?
explanation: She imagined a **memory vitamin**, Vitamin-M, to give old people to improve their memories. Grandpa had absent-mindedly taken a double dose of medicine and once got lost on a walk. He also could not see or hear well, but the vitamin she wished for was only for **memory**.

subject: english
prompt: Why did Ravi's mother lock up Grandpa's small brick house and bring him to live in the city?

image.alt: A small brick house with a big mango tree at dusk

options.text: He had sold the house to pay for his medicines
He slipped in the garden one evening and lay outside all night with no one to help him up
He had to go into hospital after taking a double dose of his medicines
He wanted to spend the school holidays teaching Ravi chess

hint: Think of what happened while he was pottering around the garden late one evening.
explanation: Grandpa had **slipped and fallen** in his garden while pottering around and lay outside all night because nobody was at home to help him up. After this, his daughter brought him to her flat because he was getting too old to live alone. The hospital stay for the double dose happened **after** he moved to the city, so it was not the reason.

subject: english
prompt: Grandpa says his old home is so quiet that **'at dusk you can even hear a leaf fall!'** Which expression is closest in meaning?

image.alt: A quiet garden at dusk with a leaf drifting down

options.text: End of one's life
Arrival of autumn
A sign of good luck
Pin-drop silence

hint: He is describing how quiet the place is, not the season.
explanation: Hearing a leaf fall means the place is completely silent. **Pin-drop silence** means it is so quiet that you could hear a pin drop. 'Arrival of autumn' is tempting because leaves fall in autumn, but Grandpa is comparing the peace of his town with the **noise and bustle** of the city.

subject: english
prompt: Put these events of Grandpa's day out in the order in which they happened.

image.alt: Passengers seen through the windows of a moving city bus

items.text: Grandpa sips sugary tea and eats two bananas and an ice cream
Ravi jumps on a bus and finds a stranger wearing Grandpa's cap
Grandpa sets off, saying he will fetch the Tamil newspaper
Ravi is thrown out of the Ladies' Hairdressing Salon
Grandpa buys peanuts and watches the children play in the park
Grandpa crosses the road and enters the barber shop

hint: Grandpa's first stop was the park; the bus came at the very end.
explanation: Grandpa left for the **Tamil newspaper**, stopped at the **park** for peanuts, then had forbidden treats at the **tea stall**. He crossed the road into the **barber shop**, while Ravi ducked into the shop next door, a **Ladies' Hairdressing Salon**, and was thrown out. Ravi then chased a yellow cap onto a **bus**, only to find a stranger wearing it.

subject: english
prompt: This street plan shows the places on Grandpa's outing. Tap the place where Grandpa enjoyed treats that were **banned at home**.

image.alt: A street plan of the neighbourhood with numbered markers on the places

hint: Ravi watched from behind a big banyan tree while loud vendors questioned him.
explanation: At the **tea stall** under the banyan tree, Grandpa sipped a **sugary** cup of tea (sugar was forbidden at home), ate two **bananas** (another banned item) and then an **ice cream** from the cart. Ravi, hiding behind the tree, was surrounded by vendors who thought he wanted their spot.

subject: english
prompt: Tap the shop where Grandpa handed his **yellow cap** to a stranger.

image.alt: A street plan of the neighbourhood with numbered markers on the places

hint: Grandpa was as bald as a table-tennis ball, yet he went into this shop.
explanation: The stranger on the bus said that a kind old gentleman in the **barber shop** had insisted he take the cap because it was a hot day. Ravi had been thrown out of the **Ladies' salon** next door, so he never saw the cap change heads. He followed the yellow cap, not Grandpa.

subject: english
prompt: Grandpa took out a gift, and Ravi's mother reminded him that Ravi's birthday was three months ago. A moment later she **flushed** and gave a shocked, guilty look at the calendar. Why?

image.alt: A wall calendar with a date circled in red, and a gift-wrapped parcel

options.text: She realised she had bought Ravi the wrong present
She realised it was her father's own birthday, which she had circled on the calendar and then forgotten
She was annoyed that Grandpa had wasted money on gifts
She noticed that Grandpa had written the wrong date on the parcel

hint: Grandpa always gives gifts to every child in the house on a special day. Whose special day?
explanation: Grandpa's custom is to give a gift to every 'child' in the house on **his own birthday**. At the start of the year Ravi's mother had circled that date in red, yet she forgot it. So the person who doubted Grandpa's memory was the one who had forgotten, which made her **flush** (turn red) with embarrassment.

subject: english
prompt: 'My daughter needs some Vitamin-M, I think—for her memory.' Why is this remark by Grandpa so funny?

image.alt: A family in their living room with an old man in a rocking chair

options.text: It turns her own wish back on her: she wanted a memory vitamin for old people, yet she forgot his birthday
Grandpa has mixed up his daughter with his late wife
Grandpa is asking her to buy him more medicine
Grandpa is complaining that the tablets she gives him do not work

hint: Remember who first wished for Vitamin-M, and for whom.
explanation: This is **irony**: the roles are reversed. Ravi's mother wished for Vitamin-M to help old people like Grandpa remember, but she is the one who forgot his birthday. The remark also shows Grandpa's sharp, witty mind, which is the opposite of the forgetful old man she believed him to be.

subject: english
prompt: Grandpa gives Ravi *The Best Detective Stories* and says it will teach him 'how to avoid getting fooled when one is **trailing** a suspect'. What does this suggest?

image.alt: A thick book of detective stories with a magnifying glass

options.text: Grandpa had forgotten Ravi's birthday and picked any book in a hurry
Grandpa wants Ravi to choose a career in the police
Grandpa now enjoys detective stories more than chess
Grandpa had probably noticed Ravi following him and enjoyed tricking him

hint: 'Trailing' means following. Who was trailing whom that morning?
explanation: **Trailing** means following. Grandpa's remark about not getting fooled while trailing a suspect hints that he knew Ravi had followed him and been fooled by the cap he gave away. Ravi is left wondering whether the twinkle in Grandpa's eye is innocent or **mischievous**. Ravi's father, who knows nothing, simply asks whether Ravi wants to be a detective.

subject: english
prompt: At the start, Grandpa seems to be losing his memory. Which **THREE** details from the story show that his mind is actually sharp?

image.alt: A chessboard with a game in progress and a large white knight

options.text: He recalls famous chess games, such as moves by Karpov, Fischer and Spassky
He once took a double dose of his medicines
He remembers his own birthday and his custom of giving gifts on it
He forgets the names of people he meets often
He finds his way home alone and is asleep before Ravi gets back
He once got lost on a walk and forgot the way home

hint: Choose only the details that prove a good memory, not the ones that worried his daughter.
explanation: Grandpa remembers **thousands of chess games**, recalls his **birthday** when his daughter has forgotten it, and **finds his way home** on his own after the outing. The double dose, the forgotten names and getting lost are the worries his daughter had, so they support the idea of a failing memory instead of disproving it.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A boy peeping round a wall at an old man in a yellow cap

assertion: Ravi decided to follow Grandpa secretly, at a safe distance.
reason: If Ravi insisted on going with Grandpa, Grandpa would feel hurt. If he let Grandpa go alone, Ravi's mother would be furious.
hint: A dilemma is a difficult choice between two options. How did Ravi try to avoid both bad results?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Ravi was in a **dilemma**: Grandpa would feel hurt if Ravi insisted on going with him, and his mother would be furious if he let Grandpa go out alone. Following **secretly** seemed to keep Grandpa safe without hurting his pride.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A book of detective stories with a magnifying glass and footprints

assertion: Grandpa had no idea that Ravi was following him around the town.
reason: When Grandpa gave his gift, he made a remark about not getting fooled while trailing a suspect.
hint: Does the remark about trailing a suspect sound like someone who noticed nothing?
explanation: A is false and R is true. Grandpa's comment about **trailing a suspect**, and his cool complaint that Ravi 'just disappeared' instead of looking after him, suggest he knew exactly what Ravi had been doing. The story ends with a **mischievous** twinkle in his eye.

subject: english
prompt: Match each statement from the story with its speaker. One speaker is extra.

image.alt: Coloured speech bubbles above a row of people

left.text: "This area is booked by us. There's no room for any new vendors."
"How dare you shoo my child? Who are you?"
"Whatever happens, Ravi, you're not to let Grandpa go out on his own."
"I hope you're not going to be as tiresome as your mother, Ravi."
"Are you playing hide and seek? I can show you a better place to hide."

right.text: The small child in the park

hint: The vendors spoke at the tea stall; the umbrella-waving lady and the curious child were in the park.
explanation: The **comb-seller** at the tea stall thought Ravi wanted her spot. In the park, the **small child** offered a better hiding place and his **mother** scolded Ravi for shooing him. **Ravi's mother** gave the strict instruction before work, and **Grandpa** called her 'tiresome' for treating him like a baby. The stranger on the bus only explained, in reported words, how he got the cap.

subject: english
prompt: A Critical Reflection question asks about **bias based on age**. Which moment shows Grandpa being treated as less able only because he is old?

image.alt: A woman talking to an old man in a rocking chair while a boy looks on

options.text: Grandpa insists on walking to the corner shop by himself
Ravi's father usually buys the Tamil paper on his way home
Ravi's mother speaks to him in an over-loud tone, as if to a child who cannot hear or understand
The stranger accepts Grandpa's cap because it is a hot day

hint: Ravi **winced** at this moment.
explanation: Ravi **winced** (showed embarrassment) at the **over-loud tone** his mother used, as though Grandpa were a child who could not understand. Grandpa himself protests about being treated 'like a baby' and kept 'a prisoner'. Walking to the shop alone shows his **independence**, not bias against him.

subject: english
topic: Reflect and respond: caring for the elderly
prompt: Look at the **'Caring for the Elderly'** organiser. Which pair correctly matches a problem Grandpa faced with its reason, as shown in the story?

image.alt: A graphic organiser about caring for the elderly with four boxes

options.text: Problem: he lay hurt in his garden all night. Reason: he lived alone with no one at home to help
Problem: he got lost on a walk. Reason: the city was too quiet for him
Problem: he took a double dose of medicine. Reason: Ravi gave him the wrong tablets
Problem: he hated the poky little flat. Reason: he had forgotten his old address

hint: Which problem happened in his own town, before he moved?
explanation: Living **alone** meant no one could help when Grandpa slipped and fell, so he lay outside all night. That is why his daughter brought him to the city. The city was **noisy and crowded**, not quiet; the double dose was his own absent-mindedness; and he disliked the flat because it was small, not because he forgot his address.

subject: english
prompt: At the end of **'The Lost Child'**, a kind man offers the crying boy a ride, music, a balloon, a garland and sweets, but he refuses them all. What is the message of this ending?

image.alt: A small boy crying in a crowd while a hand reaches down to him

options.text: Children are usually rude to strangers who try to help
Once he lost his parents, nothing he had longed for mattered; their love meant more than any toy
The fair was too crowded and noisy for anyone to enjoy
The man was only offering things that were cheap and coarse

hint: Compare what the child wanted before he was lost with what he wanted after.
explanation: Before he was lost, the child longed for burfi, a garland, balloons, music and a ride. After losing his parents he only sobbed, **'I want my mother, I want my father!'** Mulk Raj Anand shows that a child's sense of **security and love** matters far more than material things.

subject: english
prompt: Tap the thing the child was asking to ride when he turned round and found that his parents were **gone**.

image.alt: A village fair scene with numbered markers on the stalls and rides

hint: Men, women and children were whirling on it, shrieking with dizzy laughter.
explanation: Watching the **roundabout** in full swing, the child made a bold request to ride it. There was no reply: his parents were not ahead of him, beside him or behind him. Panic-stricken, he ran in all directions, and his yellow turban came untied.

subject: english
topic: The Lost Child: the child's wishes
prompt: Before he got lost, the child wanted many things, but he moved on from each one without waiting for an answer. Match each thing with the reason he thought his parents would give for saying no.

image.alt: A colourful village fair with stalls and a roundabout

right.text: He was too old to play with such toys
It was coarse, and he was forbidden to hear it
They would say it was cheap

hint: Each refusal either described the child (what he was or would be called) or described the thing itself.
explanation: The child knew his parents would call him **greedy** for wanting burfi and would say the garland was **cheap**. They would say he was **too old** for balloons, and they had forbidden him to hear the snake-charmer's **coarse** music. So each time he moved on, until he reached the roundabout.

subject: english
topic: The Lost Child: the kind man
prompt: After lifting the lost child out of the crowd, the kind man tried to comfort him. Arrange his offers in the order he made them.

image.alt: A boy crying among the legs of a crowd

items.text: A rainbow-coloured balloon
Sweets from the sweet shop counter
A ride on a horse at the roundabout
A garland from the flower-seller at the gate
The snake-charmer's music

explanation: The man first took him to the **roundabout**, then to the **snake-charmer**, the **balloons**, the **flower-seller** at the gate and finally the **sweet shop**. This is the child's earlier path in reverse. Each time the child refused and only sobbed for his mother and father.

subject: english
topic: The Lost Child: on the way to the fair
prompt: Arrange these moments from the child's walk to the fair in the order they happen in the story.

Lags behind, fascinated by the toys in the shops
Reaches the fair and longs for burfi at the sweetmeat seller's
Tries to catch dragonflies over the mustard field
Runs in wild capers round the banyan tree
Is left behind watching insects and worms on the footpath

hint: The shops come first; the grove has the petals, the doves and the banyan tree.
explanation: The child lingered by the **toy shops**, chased **dragonflies** over the mustard field, watched **insects** on the footpath, gathered **petals** in the grove until the doves distracted him, and ran **capers round the banyan tree**. Then his parents led him along the footpath to the **fair**. Each time, his parents called, 'Come, child, come!'

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A village fair with a balloon seller and a roundabout

assertion: When the man offered him a rainbow-coloured balloon, the child turned his eyes away and only sobbed.
reason: The child believed that balloons were cheap things his parents disliked.
hint: Check which item the parents would have called 'cheap'.
explanation: A is true: the child turned his eyes from the balloons and sobbed for his parents. R is false: he expected his parents to say he was **too old** to play with such toys, while it was the **garland** they would call cheap. In any case, once he was lost he wanted nothing but his mother and father.

subject: english
topic: Poem: I Cannot Remember My Mother
prompt: In stanza 3 of **'I Cannot Remember My Mother'**, the poet looks out of his bedroom window. He feels that the stillness of his mother's gaze has spread all over something. Tap it.

image.alt: A child's bedroom with numbered markers on things in the room

hint: He sends his eyes into the distant blue.
explanation: The poet sends his eyes 'into the blue of the distant **sky**' and feels the stillness of his mother's gaze has spread all over it. This is **visual imagery**, and the vast, calm sky becomes a **symbol** of her loving presence all around him.

subject: english
prompt: On an early autumn morning, the fragrance of something comes to the poet as **the scent of his mother**. Tap it.

image.alt: A child's bedroom with numbered markers on things in the room

hint: They are small white flowers with orange stalks, also called coral jasmine.
explanation: In stanza 2 the smell of **shiuli flowers** (coral jasmine, also called Parijat or Harsingar) floats in the autumn air, along with the scent of the morning service in the temple. Together they bring back 'the scent of my mother'. This is **olfactory** imagery, appealing to the sense of smell.

subject: english
prompt: Each stanza begins with **'I cannot remember my mother'**. Why does the poet use this line as a refrain?

image.alt: A child's bedroom with a cradle, toys and a window open to the sky

options.text: To show that he has forgotten her completely and no longer misses her
To create a regular rhyme scheme for the poem
To list the events of her life in the order they happened
To stress his loss, while each stanza shows how a sound, a scent or a sight still brings her close

hint: A refrain is a line repeated at regular intervals. What follows it each time?
explanation: A **refrain** is a line repeated at regular intervals. Each time the poet says he cannot remember her, the stanza goes on to show her presence returning through a **tune**, a **scent** or the **sky**. The repetition deepens the feeling of **longing**. The poem has no rhyme scheme, so the refrain is not there to make rhymes.

subject: english
prompt: 'only sometimes in the midst of my play / a tune seems to hover over my playthings' — What role does the hovering tune play?

image.alt: A rocking cradle with musical notes floating over toys

options.text: It makes his games more exciting
It interrupts and spoils his playtime
It awakens memories of his mother, who hummed it while rocking his cradle
It stands for the carefree nature of childhood

hint: Read the next line of the stanza: whose song was it?
explanation: The tune is the song his mother used to **hum** while rocking his cradle, so it **activates memories** of her. To **hover** is to linger near a place, and the word 'sometimes' shows the memory comes only now and then. The tune does not change his games; it brings his mother close.

subject: english
prompt: Which word from stanza 1 of the poem is an example of **onomatopoeia**?

image.alt: A cradle rocking while musical notes float in the air

options.text: hum
hover
cradle
tune

hint: Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like the sound it describes.
explanation: **Onomatopoeia** is a word that imitates the sound it names. **Hum**, singing a tune with the lips closed, sounds like the low 'mmm' it describes. 'Hover', 'cradle' and 'tune' are ordinary words whose sound does not copy their meaning.

subject: english
prompt: In Thomas Hood's poem **'I Remember, I Remember'**, which **THREE** of these word pairs rhyme at the ends of its lines?

image.alt: A cottage window with the sun peeping in and flowers below

options.text: born – morn
white – light
sun – soon
set – yet
window – robin
lilacs – laburnum

hint: Say each pair aloud. Rhyming words share the same ending sound, not just the same first letter.
explanation: In each group of four lines the **second and fourth lines rhyme**: born–morn, white–light and set–yet. 'Sun' and 'soon' look alike but have different vowel sounds, and 'window–robin' and 'lilacs–laburnum' do not share an ending sound at all. In the same poem the sun is **personified** as 'He' who came 'peeping in at morn', and the mood is **nostalgic**.

subject: english
prompt: 'Off he went, twirling his walking stick jauntily, leaving Ravi in a **dilemma**.' Which two synonyms of 'dilemma' complete the letter tiles?

image.alt: Letter tiles: DILEMMA above two words with missing letters

options.text: quantity, precedent
quandary, predicament
quietly, prediction
quarrel, prominent

hint: Both words describe a difficult situation in which it is hard to decide what to do.
explanation: A **dilemma** is a situation in which you must choose between two difficult options. **Quandary** (QU-A-ND-AR-Y) and **predicament** (PR-E-D-I-C-A-M-E-NT) fit the tiles and share that meaning. Ravi was stuck: going along would hurt Grandpa, and staying back would anger his mother. The other words neither fit the tiles nor mean a difficult choice.

prompt: The vocabulary task puts words into two groups: **movement words** and **sound words**. Tap the card that is a **sound** word.

image.alt: Five word cards from the story with numbered markers

hint: Which word could you hear rather than see?
explanation: 'His heart **thudded** anxiously': a **thud** is a dull, heavy sound. The other cards show movement: **crouch** (bend low), **darted** (moved or looked quickly), **sprinting** (running very fast) and **twirling** (spinning round).

subject: english
prompt: Which of these words from the story are **movement** words? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A boy creeping on all fours behind park benches

options.text: crawl
boomed
zigzagging
whirr
sprinting
grunted

hint: Picture each word: can you see it happen, or only hear it?
explanation: **Crawl** (move on hands and knees), **zigzagging** (moving in sharp turns, as Grandpa did through traffic) and **sprinting** (running very fast) describe movement. **Boomed**, **whirr** and **grunted** are sound words: the lady's loud voice boomed, Grandpa's snoring was a gentle whirr, and he grunted in his sleep.

subject: english
prompt: Match each word from the story with its meaning. One meaning is extra.

image.alt: Five cartoon faces showing different feelings

right.text: badly affected by an unpleasant feeling
an expression of emotion, such as a look in the eyes

hint: Ravi's mother 'flushed' and gave a 'stricken' look; Grandpa 'countered' her question.
explanation: Ravi looked **embarrassed** (uncomfortable) when Grandpa complained about him. Grandpa **countered** (replied to an argument) with 'Have you forgotten?', and Ravi's mother **flushed** (turned red) with a **stricken** look (badly affected by an unpleasant realisation). Ravi wondered whether the **gleam** in Grandpa's eye was innocent or mischievous. 'To be confused' is the extra meaning.

subject: english
prompt: These sensory words are from the poem's vocabulary task. Match each word with the sense it is linked to.

image.alt: An eye
An ear
A nose
A hand

hint: Ask yourself: would I see it, hear it, smell it or feel it?
explanation: **Crimson** is a deep red colour you see (visual). **Sizzle** is the hissing sound of food frying (auditory). **Pungent** describes a strong, sharp smell (olfactory), and **fluffy** describes something soft to touch (tactile). Poets use such words to create **imagery**.

subject: english
topic: Vocabulary: sensory words in a passage
prompt: In a passage by Sarojini Naidu, little birds are 'bursting with the ______ ecstasy of life in nesting time'. Which sensory word fits the blank best?

image.alt: A spring morning with singing birds on a branch and red lilies

options.text: sizzle
smooth
shrill
scents

hint: Birds in nesting time are noisy. You need an adjective describing a sound.
explanation: **Shrill** means high-pitched and piercing, the right auditory word for excited birdsong, and it fits before 'ecstasy' as an adjective. **Sizzle** is a frying sound used as a verb or noun, **smooth** appeals to touch, and **scents** is a noun about smell.

subject: english
prompt: Prepositions show how a noun or pronoun is related to other words in a sentence. Tap the **preposition** in this sentence from the story (read the cards from top to bottom).

image.alt: A sentence from the story split into numbered word cards

hint: Which word tells you where Ravi was in relation to the tree?
explanation: **Behind** is a preposition of place. It links 'position' to 'a big banyan tree' and tells us where Ravi stood. 'Ravi' and 'position' are nouns, 'took' is a verb, and 'a big' is an article with an adjective.

subject: english
prompt: Choose the correct preposition: 'I walked through the village and crossed a bridge ______ a brook.'

image.alt: A small arched bridge, a brook and a cottage

options.text: under
beside
through
over

hint: Where is a bridge in relation to the water it crosses?
explanation: A bridge goes across and above water, so we say a bridge **over** a brook. 'Under' would put the bridge below the water, 'beside' would mean it does not cross the brook at all, and 'through' would mean wading in the water. The preposition shows **position** and **direction**.

subject: english
prompt: 'Has she told you not to let me go out on my own?' asked Grandpa. What kind of sentence is the question in quotes?

image.alt: A woman talking to an old man in a rocking chair while a boy looks on

options.text: A Wh- type interrogative sentence
A Yes/No type interrogative sentence
An exclamatory sentence
An imperative sentence

hint: Look at the first word. Can the question be answered with a simple yes or no?
explanation: The question begins with the helping verb **'Has'** and can be answered 'yes' or 'no', so it is a **Yes/No type** interrogative sentence. A Wh- type question begins with a word such as who, what, where or how. It is not exclamatory (it does not express strong feeling) or imperative (it is not an order).

subject: english
prompt: Which of these questions from the unit are **Wh- type** interrogative sentences? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Question cards falling into two sorting boxes

options.text: Who are you?
Shall we play chess or watch the cricket match on TV?
What did you both do today?
Are you playing hide and seek?
How did you get here, child?
Have you forgotten?

hint: Check the first word of each question.
explanation: **Who**, **What** and **How** questions ask for information, so they are Wh- type interrogatives. The questions beginning with the helping verbs **Shall**, **Are** and **Have** are not Wh- type: 'Are you playing…?' and 'Have you forgotten?' are Yes/No questions, and 'Shall we play chess or watch the cricket match?' asks the listener to pick one of two choices.

subject: english
prompt: A small child asked Ravi, "Are you playing hide and seek?" Choose the correct **reported speech**.

image.alt: A children's park with a swing, a bench and an elephant-shaped bush

options.text: The small child asked Ravi if he was playing hide and seek.
The small child asked Ravi if he is playing hide and seek.
The small child asked Ravi if was he playing hide and seek.
The small child asked Ravi that was I playing hide and seek.

hint: Yes/No question: add 'if' or 'whether', shift the tense back and change the question into a statement.
explanation: For a **Yes/No** question, use **if/whether** after the reporting verb, make it a **statement** (subject before verb), change 'you' to **he** and shift the present continuous 'are playing' to the past continuous **'was playing'**. Keeping 'is playing' forgets the tense shift, 'if was he' keeps the question word order, and 'that was I' uses the wrong joining word and the wrong pronoun.

subject: english
prompt: Ravi's mother asked, "What did you both do today?" Choose the correct **reported speech**.

image.alt: A family in their living room in the evening

options.text: Ravi's mother asked them what did they both do that day.
Ravi's mother asked them what they both did today.
Ravi's mother asked them what they had both done that day.
Ravi's mother asked them if they had both done that day.

hint: Keep the Wh- word, then use statement order, past perfect and 'that day'.
explanation: For a **Wh-** question, keep the same Wh- word (**what**) after the reporting verb and use statement word order. The simple past 'did … do' becomes the **past perfect** 'had done', 'you' becomes **they**, and 'today' becomes **that day**. 'What did they both do' keeps the question order, 'did today' misses the tense and time changes, and 'if they had both done' wrongly replaces 'what' with 'if'.

subject: english
prompt: Priya asked Arvind, "Do you have grandparents living with you?" Choose the correct **reported speech**.

image.alt: Two classmates chatting beside a calendar and a pill box

options.text: Priya asked Arvind whether you have grandparents living with you.
Priya asked Arvind whether he has grandparents living with him.
Priya asked Arvind did he have grandparents living with him.
Priya asked Arvind whether he had grandparents living with him.

hint: Change the pronouns to fit Arvind, shift 'have' back one tense, and drop the helping verb 'do'.
explanation: This Yes/No question needs **whether** (or if). The pronouns change (**you → he**, **you → him**) and the simple present 'have' shifts to the simple past **'had'**. Keeping 'you' changes nothing, 'he has' forgets the tense shift, and 'did he have' keeps the question form.

subject: english
prompt: Match each word or form in **direct speech** with the form it usually takes in **indirect (reported) speech**.

image.alt: A speech bubble with quotation marks and an arrow to a notebook

hint: Reported speech moves words further away in time and place, and moves tenses one step back.
explanation: When words are reported at another time and place, **today → that day**, **tomorrow → the following day**, **now → then** and **here → there**. Tenses move one step back, so the simple past **did** becomes the past perfect **had done**. These are the guidelines given in the unit's table.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A wall calendar with a date circled in red, and a gift parcel

assertion: In reported speech, Grandpa's question "Have you forgotten?" is introduced with 'if' or 'whether' after the reporting verb.
reason: It is a Yes/No type question, so there is no Wh- word to place after the reporting verb.
hint: Which kind of question needs 'if' or 'whether'?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. A **Yes/No** question has no Wh- word, so we join it with **if/whether**: 'Grandpa asked her if she had forgotten.' The present perfect 'have forgotten' also shifts back to the past perfect **'had forgotten'**.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A speech bubble with quotation marks and an arrow to a notebook

assertion: When direct speech is reported, 'today' usually changes to 'that day'.
reason: In a reported Wh- question, the same Wh- word is placed next to the reporting verb.
hint: Both statements are rules from the unit. Does the second one explain the first?
explanation: Both statements are true but R does not explain A. 'Today' becomes **'that day'** because the words are reported at a different **time**. The rule about keeping the **Wh- word** concerns how questions are joined, not time words.

prompt: The Speaking Activity explains **intonation**. Which pitch pattern should you use for a question that offers a choice, such as 'Shall we play chess or watch the cricket match on TV?'

image.alt: A chessboard with a game in progress

options.text: Pattern P

image.alt: Pitch pattern P

options.text: Pattern Q

image.alt: Pitch pattern Q

options.text: Pattern R

image.alt: Pitch pattern R

options.text: Pattern S

image.alt: Pitch pattern S

hint: The voice goes up on the first choice and comes down on the last one.
explanation: A question with **choices** uses a **rise-fall** intonation: the voice rises on 'chess' and falls on 'cricket match'. Wh- and How questions use a line that **falls** at the end, and Yes/No questions use a line that **rises** at the end. A line that stays flat sounds dull and gives the listener no clue.

image.alt: A school magazine cover with an old man and a boy, and a pen

items.text: How the elderly inspire: examples, facts and quotations
The title of the article
A final comment and the most important ideas to think about
A brief introduction to the main idea, without details
Your name and grade
How they overcame challenges, and their impact on you

hint: The title goes at the top with your name and grade below it.
explanation: An article opens with a **title** and the writer's **name and grade**. subject: english
prompt: The diary-entry task notes that Anne Frank and Zlata Filipovic began their entries with 'Dear diary', but **Samuel Pepys** did not. Why not?

image.alt: An open diary being written in with a pen

options.text: He wrote his diary only in the third person
He saw his diary as a record of facts, thoughts and feelings, not as a friend
He wrote only one entry every year
His diary had no space at the top of each page

hint: Anne Frank and Zlata thought of their diaries as friends.
explanation: Anne Frank and Zlata Filipovic treated their diaries as **friends**, so they addressed them as 'Dear diary'. Samuel Pepys saw his diary as a **documentation of facts**, thoughts and feelings, so he did not. Either way, a diary entry begins with the **day, date and time**, uses the **first person**, includes sensory details and emotions, and ends with a **reflection**.

subject: english
prompt: In the Speaking Activity you give a presentation about a time you cared for an older person. Arrange the parts in the order the prompts suggest.

image.alt: A young person helping an elderly woman on a walk, beside a presentation board

items.text: What you learned about the older person: 'Their challenges offered insights into the difficulties of ageing, such as…'
Background of the experience: 'The person I had the privilege of taking care of was…'
What you learned about yourself: 'In this role, I learned that I possess the ability to…'

hint: First say who you cared for, then what you discovered.
explanation: The prompts start with the **background** (who you cared for and when), move to **what you learned about yourself**, such as new strengths and personal growth, and end with **what you learned about the older person**: their needs, preferences and the challenges of ageing. This order takes the listener from the event to its meaning.
